gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many blood pressure readings each device gets per charge. From the makers' battery test conditions: Huawei Watch D2 and D3 get about 36 cuff readings per charge at 6 a day for 6 days, and up to 96 when 24-hour ABPM (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring) is on at 15-minute intervals, though then the battery lasts only 1 day. Omron HeartGuide gets about 16 cuff readings per charge at 8 a day for 2 days. Hilo Core gets up to 210–525 optical estimates, and none of those are cuff readings.
standout_why: I compared against the pages ChatGPT cited and the top results it got. us.hilo.com (Hilo Core vs HLTH vs Hume) lists prices, 35 readings a day and 30-day calibration, but its battery entry for Hilo Core says 'Not stated'. fitcoin.co already does the cost math (Hilo Core costs $239.98 in year one and $539.96 over three years), so cost per year is taken. Its own table, though, says readings per charge 'cannot be calculated' for any device. I couldn't open the Wareable Watch D3 review (HTTP 403). The other pages ChatGPT cited are an FDA safety notice, Samsung's announcement, the ESH consensus and Android Authority, and all of them are about accuracy or regulation. None gives battery life tied to how often you take a BP reading.
decides: This confirms the Huawei Watch D2/D3 as the pick for someone who wants many real cuff readings and still a weeklong battery: about 36 cuff readings per charge, against about 16 for the Omron HeartGuide, which also has to be charged about every 2 days. It also exposes a catch the answers miss. A full 24-hour ABPM session runs the Huawei battery down to about 1 day, and Expert Reviews' Jonathan Bray saw about 3 days when testing 'multiple times per day'. Hilo Core gives far more readings per charge, but they are optical estimates checked against a cuff, not cuff readings. The figure helps choose a watch but does not overturn the medical caveat.

findings.note: Bray took 6 readings in one sample day. Against an AND UA767S-W cuff, his average difference was 2.8 mmHg systolic and 1.8 mmHg diastolic. Reviewed price £399.

findings.note: 35 a day max × 6 days = 210; 35 × 15 days = 525. Hilo doesn't link its battery range to the 35-a-day maximum, so this is a ceiling. The band isn't FDA-cleared; only the included arm cuff is, and it calibrates the band every 30 days.

unsourced: Omron HeartGuide battery spec from Omron itself: omron-healthcare.com/products/heartguide returned 403, the US FAQ page loaded without HeartGuide content, both Omron fact-sheet PDFs returned 404, and I couldn't download the BP8000-M manual PDF (certificate error, and shell download wasn't permitted).
Huawei Watch D2/D3 ABPM night interval, which would turn the 96-reading ceiling into an exact count: Huawei's spec pages say only '15-min intervals'.
Hilo Core battery life at a stated number of estimates per day: Hilo's FAQ gives a 6–15 day range without a measurement rate.

Samsung Galaxy Watch8/9 and Apple Watch Series 11: their BP features are spot estimates or notifications and aren't part of any battery test condition, so readings per charge can't be worked out from maker figures.
Current US prices for the candidates: I didn't check them because cost per year is already on fitcoin.co. With prices, a cost-per-cuff-reading figure would be possible.
